275	## Financials and capital efficiency: the 2026 standard
276	
277	### 1. Runway planning must be explicit
278	- Plan **18–24 months** of cash burn before needing new capital (Carta).
279	- Reality: many companies won't hit the next round in 18 months. SaaStr/Carta: seed-to-A stretches to 3+ years for many companies.
280	- **Deck implication:** your "ask" slide must explain not only "how much," but what that money buys and what happens if the next round takes longer.
281	
282	### 2. Include an efficiency view (especially seed+)
283	a16z: burn multiple = cash burned / net ARR added. Show a small "efficiency" box on your metrics slide:
284	- Net burn (monthly/quarterly)
285	- Net new ARR (if applicable)
286	- Burn multiple trend
287	- Gross margin trend
288	
289	Even if early, showing you track this reads as "operator," not "storyteller."
290	
291	### 3. Financial projection standards by stage
292	
293	| Stage | What to show |
294	| --- | --- |
295	| Pre-seed | 12–18 month budget, current burn, runway post-raise, hiring plan tied to milestones |
296	| Seed | Simple operating model: revenue assumptions, gross margin, burn, runway. Unit economics if measurable. 18–24 month horizon |
297	| Series A | Multi-year forecast with clear assumptions. Revenue by segment. Expense breakdown by department. Headcount plan. Cash flow. Path to profitability or next milestone. Best/base/worst scenarios |

301	## Design rules that match how investors actually read
302	
303	### Core principles
304	- **One idea per slide.** No exceptions.
305	- **Big type; minimal paragraphs.** 24pt+ body text minimum.
306	- **Charts over text** for traction (growth line, cohorts, funnel).
307	- **Avoid complex diagrams** unless they are instantly legible.
308	- **Put strongest proof earlier** than you feel comfortable doing.
309	- **Consistent design language:** 2–3 primary colors, 1–2 fonts, generous white space.
310	
311	### Mobile readability is required (not mobile-shaped)
312	- Storydoc: **32%** of decks are opened on mobile (broader surveys cite up to 70% for initial scans).
313	- Keep standard 16:9 format but enforce a "phone test": big fonts, minimal text, charts readable without zoom.
314	- Do not switch to 9:16 portrait as a default—it's emerging but not standard.
315	
316	### Appendix strategy
317	- DocSend: appendix can distract or introduce objections early.
318	- **Clean approach:** core deck for the meeting, separate deep-dive materials on request.
319	- Don't assume investors will read the appendix.
320	
321	### Pre-send checklist
322	- Deck tells story without narration (email version)
323	- All data is accurate and current
324	- Zero typos (use AI tools to verify)
325	- All charts have clear labels and sources
326	- All links work
327	- Financial projections have clear, defensible assumptions
328	- Contact information visible and correct
329	- File name is professional (CompanyName_PitchDeck_Month2026.pdf)
330	- PDF optimized for file size (< 10MB)
331	- Tested on desktop and mobile

335	## Common mistakes that reliably kill momentum
336	
337	| Mistake | Fix |
338	| --- | --- |
339	| Purpose statement is vague or buzzwordy | One declarative sentence + measurable outcome |
340	| Problem is "nice to have" | Show urgency, budget owner, and cost of inaction |
341	| Competition slide is missing or dishonest | Include alternatives + plan to win; investors scrutinize this section more than you think |
342	| No product evidence | Demo link, screenshots, pilot workflow — "Minimum Viable PowerPoint" is no longer enough |
343	| Ask is "we need money to grow" | Money → milestones → next financing / "default alive" plan |
344	| Overloading slides with dense text | Design for skimming; you have ~2:30 of real attention |
345	| Hype without proof | "Uber for X" positioning, inflated TAM, hockey sticks without explanation |
346	| Ignoring stage fit | Don't use a pre-seed deck structure for Series A |
347	| Features instead of outcomes | Focus on value delivered, not technical architecture |
348	| Outdated fundraising ranges | Know the current benchmarks; signals market awareness |

352	## The practical build process
353	
354	1. **Write the 10-line narrative first (no slides).** Use Sequoia's order: purpose → problem → solution → why now → market → competition → model → team → financials.
355	2. **Turn each line into a slide headline that states a conclusion.** Not "Market" but "The compliance automation market is $8B and growing 22% YoY."
356	3. **Attach one proof point to every slide.** Proof = data, customer quote, screenshot, benchmark, signed LOI, cohort chart, or a clear decision.
357	4. **Cut ruthlessly.** Every slide must earn its place given ~2:30 of attention.
358	5. **Build the data room in parallel.** Cap table and historical burn/P&L ready for diligence.
359	6. **Test the deck.** Give it to someone unfamiliar with your company — they should understand it immediately. Test on mobile.

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01St5pDD25Zwfboq4rb1azib","type":"tool_result","content":"1	# Deck Review Checklist Criteria
2	
3	35 criteria across 7 categories. Each criterion has an ID, label, definition, and evidence basis (the best-practice principle it's grounded in).
4	
5	## Category 1 — Narrative Flow (5 items)
6	
7	### `purpose_clear`
8	**Label:** Company purpose is clear and specific
9	**Pass:** One declarative sentence that a smart investor can repeat after 10 seconds. Follows formats like "[Category] for [ICP] that delivers [quantified outcome]."
10	**Fail:** Purpose is vague, buzzwordy, requires multiple readings, or is missing.
11	**Warn:** Purpose exists but is two sentences or slightly unclear.
12	**Basis:** Sequoia "Writing a Business Plan" — define the company in a single declarative sentence.
13	
14	### `headlines_carry_story`
15	**Label:** Slide headlines are conclusions, not topics
16	**Pass:** Headlines state conclusions ("Retention is 92% at 6 months") rather than topics ("Retention").
17	**Fail:** Most headlines are single-word topics or generic labels.
18	**Warn:** Mixed — some headlines carry conclusions, others are topics.
19	**Basis:** DocSend/Sequoia — investors skim headlines first; each headline should be a conclusion.
20	
21	### `narrative_arc_present`
22	**Label:** Narrative follows Problem-Solution-Proof-Ask arc
23	**Pass:** Core arc follows Problem → Solution → Why now → Proof → Ask. Story feels inevitable.
24	**Fail:** No discernible narrative arc; slides feel like a data dump or random ordering.
25	**Warn:** Arc is present but has gaps or awkward transitions.
26	**Basis:** Sequoia, DocSend, YC — consistent core arc across all frameworks.
27	
28	### `strongest_proof_early`
29	**Label:** Strongest proof appears by slide 4
30	**Pass:** Best traction/proof point appears within first 4 slides. Hooks the reader.
31	**Fail:** Strongest proof is buried after slide 6.
32	**Warn:** Some proof early but the strongest evidence is mid-deck.
33	**Basis:** DocSend data — 78% abandon before slide 6, but if reader reaches slide 4, 82% finish.
34	
35	### `story_stands_alone`
36	**Label:** Deck tells story without narration
37	**Pass:** Share-deck version is self-explanatory without verbal accompaniment.
38	**Fail:** Slides are cryptic without the founder explaining them (live-deck problem in a share-deck context).
39	**Warn:** Mostly stands alone but 1-2 slides need context.
40	**Basis:** DocSend — share decks must stand alone; investors spend ~2:30 of real attention.
41	
42	## Category 2 — Slide Content (8 items)
43	
44	### `problem_quantified`
45	**Label:** Problem slide quantifies pain
46	**Pass:** Problem slide identifies the user/buyer, the moment of pain, and quantifies it (time, money, risk, regulatory exposure, missed revenue). Uses concrete examples or customer quotes.
47	**Fail:** Problem is abstract, industry-level, or unquantified.
48	**Warn:** Problem is identified but quantification is weak or generic.
49	**Basis:** Sequoia framework — identify user/buyer, moment of pain, quantify cost of inaction.
50	
51	### `solution_shows_workflow`
52	**Label:** Solution shows before→after, not feature list
53	**Pass:** Shows the "before → after" workflow change. Product screenshot or 3-step flow when possible. Focuses on value delivered.
54	**Fail:** Solution is a feature list or technical architecture diagram.
55	**Warn:** Some workflow shown but leans toward features.
56	**Basis:** Sequoia, DocSend — show workflow change, not feature list; focus on value, not architecture.
57	
58	### `why_now_has_catalyst`
59	**Label:** Why-now has genuine macro catalyst
60	**Pass:** Cites a genuine catalyst: regulatory shift, new platform primitive, behavioral change, cost curve collapse. Answers "Why wasn't this built before?"
61	**Fail:** "Why now" is missing or says "AI is hot" / generic market timing.
62	**Warn:** Catalyst is present but weak or not clearly differentiated from competitors' timing.
63	**Basis:** Sequoia — "Why wasn't this built before?" Strongest at pre-seed/seed.
64	
65	### `market_bottom_up`
66	**Label:** Market sizing uses bottom-up approach
67	**Pass:** Shows bottom-up sizing: ICP count × willingness to pay × adoption rate. Expandability as second layer.
68	**Fail:** Only shows inflated top-down TAM chart with no justification.
69	**Warn:** Has top-down with some bottom-up elements, but bottom-up not primary.
70	**Basis:** Sequoia, multiple sources — bottom-up sizing beats generic TAM charts.
71	
72	### `competition_honest`
73	**Label:** Competition section is honest and substantive
74	**Pass:** Maps direct competitors + incumbents + "do nothing" / internal build. Uses 2-3 concrete differentiators (speed, cost, distribution, data advantage, regulatory fit, switching costs).
75	**Fail:** "No competition" or missing competition slide.
76	**Warn:** Competition acknowledged but differentiators are generic or 2x2 matrix without explanation.
77	**Basis:** DocSend — VCs spent 88% more time on competition in successful decks vs. unsuccessful.
78	
79	### `business_model_clear`
80	**Label:** Business model explains money flow and margins
81	**Pass:** Pricing model clear (seat, usage, outcome, per workflow, take-rate). Who pays vs. who uses distinguished. Gross margin structure shown (especially for AI/compute-heavy products).
82	**Fail:** No business model slide or just "SaaS" with no detail.
83	**Warn:** Pricing mentioned but gross margin or buyer vs. user distinction missing.
84	**Basis:** Sequoia framework — pricing model, buyer vs. user, gross margin structure.
85	
86	### `gtm_has_proof`
87	**Label:** GTM slide has ICP, channel, and early proof
88	**Pass:** ICP + channel (PLG, sales-led, partner-led) defined. Sales cycle + ACV expectations. Early channel proof (pipeline, conversion, CAC, payback).
89	**Fail:** No GTM slide or just "we'll do marketing."
90	**Warn:** ICP and channel mentioned but no conversion data or pipeline proof.
91	**Basis:** Sequoia, DocSend — ICP + channel + early proof required.
92	
93	### `team_has_depth`
94	**Label:** Team slide demonstrates founder-market fit
95	**Pass:** Bios, photos, LinkedIn links. Founder-market fit highlighted. Complementary skills shown. Advisory board if adding real credibility.
96	**Fail:** Just names or roles without context. No photos.
97	**Warn:** Some bios but founder-market fit not explicitly addressed.
98	**Basis:** DocSend — team slide gets ~46 seconds out of ~2:30 total (~30% of attention). Storydoc: 43% of reading time on interactive decks.
99	
100	## Category 3 — Stage Fit (5 items)
101	
102	### `stage_appropriate_structure`
103	**Label:** Slide order matches stage-specific framework
104	**Pass:** Slide ordering follows the reference outline for the detected stage.
105	**Fail:** Uses wrong stage's structure (e.g., pre-seed deck with Series A cohort data expectations).
106	**Warn:** Mostly appropriate but 1-2 slides out of expected order.
107	**Basis:** All sources — pre-seed, seed, and Series A have different emphasis and ordering.
108	
109	### `stage_appropriate_traction`
110	**Label:** Traction metrics match stage expectations
111	**Pass:** Pre-seed: LOIs, waitlist, pilot data. Seed: ARR/MRR, growth, retention. Series A: cohorts, NRR, unit economics, burn multiple.
112	**Fail:** Wrong metrics for stage or no traction evidence at all.
113	**Warn:** Some appropriate metrics but missing key ones for stage.
114	**Basis:** Stage-specific guidelines — each stage has different proof requirements.
115	
116	### `stage_appropriate_financials`
117	**Label:** Financial projections match stage depth
118	**Pass:** Pre-seed: 12-18 month budget + burn + runway + hiring plan. Seed: Operating model + revenue assumptions + gross margin + runway. Series A: Multi-year forecast + revenue by segment + headcount plan + path to profitability.
119	**Fail:** No financials or wildly inappropriate depth.
120	**Warn:** Financials present but missing stage-specific elements.
121	**Basis:** a16z, Carta — financial projection standards by stage.
122	
123	### `ask_ties_to_milestones`
124	**Label:** Ask ties dollars to milestones to next round
125	**Pass:** Explicit fundraising ask + use of funds tied to milestones + next round readiness (or default-alive path). Addresses what happens if next round takes longer.
126	**Fail:** Ask is just "we need $X to grow" with no milestone plan.
127	**Warn:** Milestones mentioned but not clearly tied to dollars or next financing.
128	**Basis:** 2026 standard — tie dollars → milestones → next round readiness (or default-alive path).
129	
130	### `round_size_realistic`
131	**Label:** Fundraising amount aligns with current benchmarks
132	**Pass:** Round size within 2025/2026 benchmarks: pre-seed $250K-$2.5M, seed $2M-$6M, Series A $10M-$20M.
133	**Fail:** Round size dramatically out of range for stage (e.g., $20M pre-seed).
134	**Warn:** On the edge of typical range but not unreasonable.
135	**Basis:** PitchBook/NVCA + Carta 2025 round-size data.
136	
137	## Category 4 — Design & Readability (5 items)
138	
139	Score all 5 normally for an uploaded file (PDF/PPTX/markdown). When there is no
140	rendered page (`input_format` is `"text"` or `"markdown"` — a deck described in
141	conversation, or a PowerPoint that could not be converted), the producer script
142	forces **four** of them to `not_applicable` after you return: there is no slide to
143	assess visual design against. Do not self-gate: assess every item as usual and let
144	the producer apply the gate.
145	
146	`slide_count_appropriate` is **not** gated, and is scored in every format. Counting
147	slides is arithmetic rather than a visual judgement, and the slide count is already
148	known — so it is answerable whether or not anyone saw the deck.
149	
150	### `one_idea_per_slide`
151	**Label:** One idea per slide
152	**Pass:** Each slide communicates a single concept clearly.
153	**Fail:** Multiple slides try to cover 2-3 distinct ideas each.
154	**Warn:** Mostly single-idea but 1-2 slides are overloaded.
155	**Basis:** All design guides — one idea per slide, no exceptions.
156	
157	### `minimal_text`
158	**Label:** Big type, minimal paragraphs
159	**Pass:** 24pt+ body text minimum. Charts over text for traction. No dense paragraphs.
160	**Fail:** Small text, dense paragraphs, text-heavy slides throughout.
161	**Warn:** Mostly good but some slides have too much text.
162	**Basis:** DocSend, Storydoc — design for ~2:30 of real attention; big type, charts over text.
163	
164	### `slide_count_appropriate`
165	**Label:** Core deck is 10-12 slides
166	**Pass:** 10-12 core slides (not counting appendix).
167	**Fail:** 6 or fewer, or 19 or more core slides.
168	**Warn:** 7-9 or 13-18 slides — outside the ideal range.
169	**Basis:** Storydoc data — ~10-slide decks achieve highest completion rate (32% vs. 22% average); sharp drop-off after ~18 slides.
170	
171	### `consistent_design`
172	**Label:** Consistent visual design language
173	**Pass:** 2-3 primary colors, 1-2 fonts, generous white space. Professional and consistent throughout.
174	**Fail:** Inconsistent fonts, colors, spacing. Looks cobbled together.
175	**Warn:** Mostly consistent but some slides break the pattern.
176	**Basis:** Design rules — consistent design language with 2-3 primary colors, 1-2 fonts, generous white space.
177	
178	### `mobile_readable`
179	**Label:** Readable on mobile without zoom
180	**Pass:** Big fonts, minimal text, charts readable without zoom. Passes "phone test."
181	**Fail:** Requires zooming on mobile to read text or charts. Tiny fonts.
182	**Warn:** Mostly readable but some slides have small elements.
183	**Basis:** Storydoc — 32% of decks opened on mobile (up to 70% for initial scans). Enforce "phone test."
184	
185	## Category 5 — Common Mistakes (5 items)
186	
187	### `no_vague_purpose`
188	**Label:** No vague or buzzwordy purpose statement
189	**Pass:** Purpose is specific, measurable, and immediately understandable.
190	**Fail:** Purpose uses buzzwords ("leveraging synergies," "paradigm shift," "revolutionary platform").
191	**Warn:** Purpose is clear but could be more specific.
192	**Basis:** Common mistakes — "One declarative sentence + measurable outcome."
193	
194	### `no_nice_to_have_problem`
195	**Label:** Problem shows urgency, not a nice-to-have
196	**Pass:** Problem has urgency, a budget owner, and clear cost of inaction.
197	**Fail:** Problem is a "nice to have" with no urgency or budget owner.
198	**Warn:** Some urgency shown but cost of inaction not quantified.
199	**Basis:** Common mistakes — show urgency, budget owner, and cost of inaction.
200	
201	### `no_hype_without_proof`
202	**Label:** No hype without supporting evidence
203	**Pass:** All claims backed by data, customer quotes, or verifiable evidence.
204	**Fail:** "Uber for X" positioning, inflated TAM, hockey stick projections without explanation.
205	**Warn:** Mostly substantiated but 1-2 claims need better support.
206	**Basis:** Common mistakes — hype without proof reliably kills momentum.
207	
208	### `no_features_over_outcomes`
209	**Label:** Focuses on outcomes, not features
210	**Pass:** Focuses on value delivered and user outcomes, not technical architecture.
211	**Fail:** Primarily a feature list or technical spec.
212	**Warn:** Mix of outcomes and features; could lean more toward outcomes.
213	**Basis:** Common mistakes — features instead of outcomes.
214	
215	### `no_dodged_competition`
216	**Label:** Competition slide exists and is substantive
217	**Pass:** Competition addressed honestly with alternatives and concrete differentiators.
218	**Fail:** No competition slide, or "we have no competitors."
219	**Warn:** Competition slide exists but is superficial.
220	**Basis:** DocSend — investors scrutinize this section more than founders think.
221	
222	## Category 6 — AI Company (4 items)
223	
224	Mark all as `not_applicable` if the company is not AI-first.
225	
226	### `ai_retention_rebased`
227	**Label:** AI retention measured from Month 3
228	**Pass:** Retention analysis rebases from Month 0 to Month 3 to filter out "AI tourists."
229	**Fail:** Only shows Month 0 retention (inflated by novelty users).
230	**Warn:** Retention shown but not explicitly rebased.
231	**Basis:** a16z — analyze retention rebased from Month 3 for AI products.
232	
233	### `ai_cost_to_serve_shown`
234	**Label:** Compute economics and margin trajectory shown
235	**Pass:** COGS breakdown (inference, data, hosting, support). Shows what improves margins (caching, model optimization, routing, pricing). Path to 60%+ gross margins.
236	**Fail:** No mention of compute costs or gross margin trajectory.
237	**Warn:** Some cost awareness but no clear margin improvement path.
238	**Basis:** a16z — failure to show path to 60%+ gross margins signals unscalable model.
239	
240	### `ai_defensibility_beyond_model`
241	**Label:** Defensibility beyond "we use [foundation model]"
242	**Pass:** Shows at least one of: proprietary data / feedback loops, workflow distribution / embeddedness, regulatory/compliance moat, vertical specialization, agentic capabilities delivering transformational ROI.
243	**Fail:** Defensibility is just "we use GPT-4" or similar.
244	**Warn:** Some defensibility noted but not deeply substantiated.
245	**Basis:** a16z, multiple sources — API wrapper without moat is not defensible.
246	
247	### `ai_responsible_controls`
248	**Label:** Responsible AI / risk controls addressed
249	**Pass:** Addresses privacy & data handling, eval & monitoring, guardrails/safety, compliance roadmap (SOC2, HIPAA, etc.). One slide — not overdone.
250	**Fail:** No mention of responsible AI practices for an enterprise-facing AI product.
251	**Warn:** Brief mention but missing key elements.
252	**Basis:** a16z — reduces deal friction, especially for enterprise.
253	
254	## Category 7 — Diligence Readiness (3 items)
255	
256	### `numbers_consistent`
257	**Label:** Claims in deck are internally consistent
258	**Pass:** Revenue, customer count, growth rate, market size, and financial projections are all mutually consistent.
259	**Fail:** Numbers contradict each other across slides (e.g., different ARR on traction vs. financials slide).
260	**Warn:** Minor inconsistencies that could be rounding or presentation differences.
261	**Basis:** a16z — deck must be consistent with what you'll show in the data room.
262	
263	### `data_room_ready`
264	**Label:** Diligence materials referenced or available
265	**Pass:** Cap table + historical P&L + burn referenced or implied available. "We have a data room ready" or equivalent.
266	**Fail:** No mention of supporting materials; deck seems to exist in isolation.
267	**Warn:** Some materials implied but data room readiness not explicit.
268	**Basis:** a16z data room guide — cap table, historical P&L, burn are baseline diligence items.
269	
270	### `contact_info_present`
271	**Label:** Contact information visible and correct
272	**Pass:** Email, LinkedIn, or other contact information clearly visible (typically on cover or closing slide).
273	**Fail:** No contact information anywhere in the deck.

This deck would get a first meeting from a developer-tools investor who knows the space — the traction is real and the ICP is sharp — but it would not survive the follow-up question session, because the deck answers six questions and leaves twenty unanswered. The single thing working hardest in your favour is $8K MRR with 18% month-over-month growth and 24 paying customers at seed stage: that is a credible revenue signal, not a promise. The single thing most likely to kill the meeting before it starts is the five missing sections. An investor reading this deck cannot assess market size, understand your business model, or evaluate how you plan to grow — and in 2026, no informed investor fills those gaps on your behalf.

**What is working**

Your traction slide is the strongest slide in the deck, and that is not a small thing. $8K MRR with 18% month-over-month growth and 24 paying customers is a specific, checkable claim — not "strong early interest" or "growing pipeline." Investors can model from that. Sequoia's seed framework puts proof of early demand as one of the two things that separate fundable from not-fundable at this stage, and you have it.

Your ICP is unusually precise. "Indie SaaS founders" is a named, findable community — Indie Hackers, ProductHunt, Twitter/X, Hacker News — and the problem you are solving for them (20+ hours per week on developer tooling integration) is concrete and time-quantified. Most seed decks describe a diffuse, everyone-with-a-computer market. Yours does not.

Your team pedigree is directly relevant. Ex-Stripe engineering and ex-Notion product is exactly the background an investor wants to see behind a developer tools company. That combination says you have shipped production tooling and you understand how developers adopt products. It is a legitimate founder-market fit signal, even though the slide itself undersells it by hiding your names and not saying what you actually built at those companies.

**The highest-leverage change you can make**

Add the five missing sections before you send this to anyone. The deck currently has six slides. A seed-stage deck needs at minimum ten, and the four you are missing are not optional — they are the slides investors have trained themselves to read first. Market sizing (to assess opportunity size), competition (to assess defensibility), business model (to assess economics), go-to-market (to assess how you will grow past 24 customers), and why now (to assess timing). DocSend data consistently shows investors spend more than twice as long on competition slides in decks that result in funding than in decks that do not — and you have no competition slide at all.

The ask slide has the same gap in miniature. "Raising $1.2M seed at $8M post-money valuation" is a number without a plan. At seed stage, the ask needs to tell an investor three things: what you will do with the money, what milestones hitting with the money will prove, and what those milestones unlock for the next round. Right now the ask tells them only the number. A use-of-funds breakdown tied to milestones — "18 months: $600K engineering, $300K GTM, $300K infrastructure, targeting $30K MRR and 100 paying customers before Series A" — turns a request into a plan.

**Would an investor take the meeting?**

A developer-tools-focused investor who recognizes the traction and team pedigree probably would, yes — but they would come to the meeting ready to interrogate the gaps rather than to hear you expand on the deck. That is a harder meeting to win than one where the deck pre-answers the questions. An investor who does not already have conviction about the developer tools market will pass on this version of the deck without requesting a meeting, because they have no way to assess whether the opportunity is large enough to matter.

The short version: the deck earns a meeting on the strength of the traction, and loses it in the meeting because the five missing sections were never addressed. Fix the deck first, then send it.

**The "AI-native" claim is a credibility liability right now**

Your title slide leads with "AI-native developer tools" and the claim appears nowhere else in the deck. No AI functionality is described, no model or approach is named, no AI-specific metric is shown. In 2026, this is not a soft concern — a16z and YC explicitly flag unsubstantiated AI claims as credibility risks because investors have been burned by them. You either need to describe concretely what the AI component does (what model, what task, what outcome) on the solution slide, or remove the claim from the title entirely until you can support it. An unsubstantiated AI claim on slide one raises a question that the rest of your six-slide deck has no room to answer, and that question sits in the investor's mind for the entire read.

**Note on design and readability**

Four of the design and readability criteria were not assessed in this review because the deck reached the review as a text description rather than a rendered file. Those criteria — covering layout, visual consistency, and mobile readability — remain unscored. If you are able to share a PDF of the deck, those four criteria can be assessed in a follow-up review.

**The one positioning suggestion the checklist does not capture**

Your deck reads as a tooling company when it should read as a founder productivity company. "One CLI wrapping GitHub, Linear, Stripe, and Vercel" describes what the product is. What you should be selling is the outcome: indie SaaS founders get 20+ hours a week back and ship their first paying customer faster. The traction slide does this implicitly — revenue and growth speak to outcomes — but the solution slide, the one designed to answer "what does this do for me?", describes the architecture instead. Flip it. Sequoia's framework is explicit: the solution slide should show the before/after world change, not the technical implementation.
